summary:
Tierra del Fuego is an Argentine province and stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and the statute has not been repealed. A trans adult visitor's identity documents are therefore not gated by medical or judicial approval.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree restricting minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, reported by Reuters as a ban on those procedures for adolescents. A second decree issued at the same time governs the housing of transgender people in prison, which is directly relevant to a trans visitor's exposure to detention.

The national government has also dismantled parts of the protection machinery. President Milei eliminated the federal Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans employees hired under the Trans Labour Quota Law, which had reserved at least 1 per cent of public-sector jobs for trans people. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Violence risk is documented at record levels. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in Argentina during 2025, a record and a rise on 2024, averaging one every 38 hours. Trans women and travestis accounted for 62.5 per cent of victims (142 people), trans men for 18 against 5 in 2024, with 13 lesbians and 4 non-binary people also targeted. Some 64.8 per cent of cases (147) involved physical violence, 32 per cent occurred in police stations or penal institutions, and police involvement rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025. These figures are national and apply to this province as part of the national position.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed on 4 April 2025 by the Washington Blade said the government's policies had left the community facing a chaotic and desperate situation with heightened exposure to violence, discrimination and poverty. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains in force notwithstanding.

Protection exists alongside that deterioration. Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010 as the first country in the region to do so, and anti-discrimination protections operate through national and provincial laws. On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, but rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeal court had removed in 2020, so the gender-motivated-crime aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration for Argentina, indicating deterioration across three separate indicators even as the 2012 statute stays on the books.

The violence figures are drawn from a national monitoring body rather than provincial records, and Agencia Presentes, reporting them on 19 March 2026, described 2025 as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina. The concentration of cases in police stations and penal institutions, together with the fourfold rise in police involvement, means the state is present in a third of documented incidents rather than only responding to them.

Trans organisations in the national capital are named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, and their leadership's April 2025 assessment frames the current environment as one of organised defensive response rather than institutional support.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tierra del Fuego lose access to the institutional channel the Trans Labour Quota Law created: the 1 per cent public-sector reservation for trans workers was undermined when trans employees hired under it were dismissed and the federal Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry was eliminated.

Trans minors resident in the province fall under the February 2025 decree restricting gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, while adult residents continue to change legal gender under Law 26.743 without medical or judicial approval.

Trans people held in the province's detention facilities fall under the second February 2025 decree governing the housing of transgender prisoners. Residents who are victims of bias crime are counted in the national observatory totals, and provincial anti-discrimination law supplies a domestic redress route that visitors cannot invoke in the same way.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not record the outcome of the litigation brought by legal experts who petitioned the courts over the February 2025 decree on minors, so whether that restriction stands unmodified is not established here.

Not sourced: no Tierra del Fuego-specific data on police practice, hate-crime incidents, detention conditions, or the availability of trans-competent health services appears in the inventory; the violence and institutional findings are national figures applied to the province.

Not sourced: the inventory does not state whether the province has its own gender-recognition procedure, its own anti-discrimination statute with a named provision, or any facility-level rules on document presentation for visitors.

Unresolved: the Outright International negative assessment on organisation registration is recorded as an indicator only, with no detail in the available material on which registration rule it refers to.
